channel.title: Nature
channel.description: Nature is the foremost international weekly scientific journal in the world and is the flagship journal for Nature Portfolio. It publishes the finest peer-reviewed research in all fields of science and technology on the basis of its originality, importance, interdisciplinary interest, timeliness, accessibility, elegance and surprising conclusions. Nature publishes landmark papers, award winning news, leading comment and expert opinion on important, topical scientific news and events that enable readers to share the latest discoveries in science and evolve the discussion amongst the global scientific community.

item.title: Tropical land-use intensification reshapes biodiversity in expected and unexpected ways
item.content:encoded:
Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03602-1

Global agricultural demand has increased over the past few decades, driving land-use intensification in some of the world’s most biodiverse regions. An assessment of some 40,000 species, from soil microorganisms to vertebrates, in Sumatra, Indonesia, reveals that agricultural intensification threatens biodiversity through species loss and changes in community composition across different spatial scales.
item.dc:title: Tropical land-use intensification reshapes biodiversity in expected and unexpected ways

item.title: Poxviruses probably evolved in the digestive system of animals
item.content:encoded:
Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03436-x

Large and giant DNA viruses that infect unicellular eukaryotes are abundant in the environment but have rarely been found in the gut microbiome. The discovery of such viruses that prevail in the digestive system of humans and animals exposes a long-overlooked facet of the gut microbiome that clarifies the origin of poxviruses.
item.dc:title: Poxviruses probably evolved in the digestive system of animals

item.content:encoded:
Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03766-w

item.title: A new view of Amazonian leaf seasonality
item.content:encoded:
Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03490-5

item.dc:title: A new view of Amazonian leaf seasonality
item.dc:creator: Gerbrand Koren

item.title: Injured locusts heal or are cannibalized depending on levels of a bacterial odour molecule
item.content:encoded:
Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03599-7

When migratory locusts are injured, an odorous chemical produced by bacteria living in or on their bodies activates the immune system, helping them to fight disease-causing agents. However, when a wound is large and the chemical becomes too concentrated, it attracts cannibalistic locusts.
item.dc:title: Injured locusts heal or are cannibalized depending on levels of a bacterial odour molecule
